abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Macrophages in the brain barrier system include microglia in the brain parenchyma, border-associated macrophages at the brain’s borders, and recruited macrophages. They are responsible for neural development, maintenance of homeostasis, and orchestrating immune responses. With the rapid exploitation and development of new technologies, there is a deeper understanding of macrophages in the brain barrier system. Here we review the origin, development, important molecules, and functions of macrophages, mainly focusing on microglia and border-associated macrophages. We also highlight some advances in single-cell sequencing and significant cell markers. We anticipate that more advanced methods will emerge to study resident and recruited macrophages in the future, opening new horizons for neuroimmunology and related peripheral immune fields.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The brain barrier system includes barriers that segregate the blood from the brain parenchyma (blood–brain barrier [BBB] and blood–leptomeningeal barrier) and a barrier that segregates the blood from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (blood–CSF barrier). The system acts as an interface separating the brain parenchyma from the peripheral tissues. The cellular elements of the brain barrier system include macrophages, astrocytes, endothelial cells, perivascular cells, neurons, and vascular smooth muscle cells. The interactions among these cells modulate multiple physiological functions, including metabolite clearance, angiogenesis, vessel permeability, blood flow regulation, and nutritional support (McConnell et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2019).

According to their different abilities to exchange substances between the circulatory system and the central nervous system (CNS), the brain can be considered as a three-compartmentalized organ (De Vlaminck et al., 2022). The first compartment contains perforated blood vessels that allow blood–brain exchange and permit CNS tissue for antigen presentation and immunocyte delivery. This compartment includes choroid plexus (CP), dura mater, and circumventricular organs (Mastorakos and McGavern, 2019; Rustenhoven et al., 2021). The second compartment containing CSF is separated from the first accessible compartment by the blood–CSF barrier. The blood–CSF barrier is formed by epithelial cells and fibroblasts, acting as a selective shutter that only permits peripheral immune cells to pass through under certain conditions (Shechter et al., 2013). The last and most immunologically privileged area is the parenchyma. It is segregated from the blood by the BBB (formed by vascular endothelial cells in the brain parenchyma or in the subpial cavity) and by the blood–leptomeningeal barrier (formed by endothelial cells of the leptomeningeal microvessels in the subpial space) (Denes et al., 2024). In addition, astrocyte barriers also form the glia limitans, which contributes to segregating the parenchyma from the blood in the perivascular and subdural spaces, as well as from the CSF in the ependymal membrane (ciliated epithelial cells covering the ventricles) (Mastorakos and McGavern, 2019).

Macrophages residing in the parenchyma are microglia. About a hundred years ago, Pio Del Rio Hortega first phenotypically identified and named this cell (Ginhoux et al., 2013). Microglia originate from yolk sac (YS) precursors (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Hoeffel et al., 2015a; Ginhoux et al., 2016). These cells are totally dependent on self-renewal and receive little replenishment from the periphery (Sheng et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018). They are formed by the colonization of primitive erythromyeloid precursors (EMPs) from the 8th day of embryonic development in the brain parenchyma. In adulthood, human brain microglia slowly replenish themselves at a rate of 28% per year, and some can survive for more than 20 years, although this rate may vary across different brain regions (Réu et al., 2017, Huang et al., 2018).

Border-associated macrophages (BAMs) reside at CNS borders (Figure 1). In two studies, BAMs are referred to as CNS-associated macrophages (Castellani et al., 2023; Frosch et al., 2023). Compared with microglia, these CNS resident macrophages also originate from EMPs. Afterwards, some precursor cells differentiate into CD206+ primitive macrophages following the establishment of the BBB, which move into the meninges and choroid plexus, forming meningeal and choroidal macrophages. During the perinatal period, meningeal macrophages further migrate to form perivascular macrophages. Similar to microglia, these long-lived macrophages are repopulated exclusively through self-renewal (Ginhoux et al., 2010). Although microglia and BAMs are mainly self-renewed (Ginhoux et al., 2010), some BAMs in the dura mater and choroid plexus (CP) stroma are replaced by peripheral recruited monocytes throughout their lifetime. In adults, a portion of the dura mater and choroid plexus stromal macrophages are gradually substituted by monocytes in small amounts through the BBB, blood–leptomeningeal barrier and blood–CSF barrier. The infiltrated monocytes can further differentiate into recruited macrophages with a short lifespan and are continuously replaced through hematopoietic stem cell differentiation (Goldmann et al., 2016; Van Hove et al., 2019).

In the brain barrier system, astrocytes are located between neurons and endothelial cells. As multifunctional cells, astrocytes are closely associated with neurons and endothelial cells. Microglia make up 5%–15% of the total cells in the human brain, and they can monitor the microenvironment and initiate reaction in responses to physiological or pathological stimuli. Recruited macrophages are macrophages differentiated from infiltrated peripheral monocytes. Border-associated macrophages (BAMs) are located at the boundaries of the brain parenchyma. sec.p: The brain barrier system is closely associated with CNS resident macrophages and recruited macrophages (Figure 1). Both resident and recruited macrophages act as significant regulators of the brain during development and in homeostasis and disease (Kierdorf et al., 2019; Prinz et al., 2019). The composition of macrophages varies in compartments with different blood–brain exchange abilities. Among them, macrophages in the aforementioned first compartment are BAMs, mainly located in the perivascular regions, meninges, and choroid plexus; In the second compartment, the CSF contains a small number of monocytes but no macrophages; In the third compartment, the main macrophages are microglia. Mounting evidence indicates that microglia and BAMs show segregated transcription patterns with differential expression of numerous marker genes, showing that they are two different types of cells (Van Hove et al., 2019). The expression profiles of macrophages from different sources and locations may exert different regulatory effects on the function of the brain barrier system (Castellani et al., 2023).

Single-cell analysis has begun to reveal the diversity of brain macrophages and their responses to disease. A disease-associated microglial subtype has initially been identified in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) (Keren-Shaul et al., 2017), and afterwards in other diseases (Anderson et al., 2019; Hammond et al., 2019; Jordão et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Masuda et al., 2019; Van Hove et al., 2019; Safaiyan et al., 2021). However, the response of recruited macrophages as well as resident macrophages in the pathogenesis of CNS diseases remains largely uncovered. The extent to which monocyte-derived macrophages differ from microglia and BAMs molecularly and functionally is still not fully understood, and these processes are undoubtedly closely related to the brain barrier system. Here, we review recent findings within this context and discuss possible roles of resident and recruited macrophages under homeostasis and pathological conditions.

sec.title: Retrieval Strategy
sec.p: A computer-based online search of the PubMed database was performed to retrieve articles published up to July 31, 2024. The following key words (MeSH terms) were used for search to maximize search specificity and sensitivity: “brain barrier system;” “CNS resident macrophage;” “recruited macrophage;” “border-associated macrophage;” “single-cell RNA sequencing;” “microglia behavior;” “recruited macrophage behavior;” “experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis;” “multiple sclerosis;” and “vascular cognitive impairment.” We screened articles by title and abstract to find out the characteristics, effects, and underlying mechanism of CNS resident macrophages and recruited macrophages. No restrictions were applied to the language or study type.

sec.title: Central Nervous System Resident and Recruited Macrophage Ontogeny Related to the Brain Barrier System
sec.p: In the past several years, a series of experiments utilizing fate-mapping (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Yona et al., 2013; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015a; Sheng et al., 2015), parabiosis, and bone marrow transplantation (Ginhoux et al., 2010) has proved the YS ontogeny of microglia. Microglia originate from YS EMPs. YS macrophages, generated from the EMPs migrate to and colonize the embryonic brain (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015); though, the character and timing of the emergence of these EMPs remain elusive (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Kierdorf et al., 2015; Perdiguero et al., 2016).

At least three waves of hematopoiesis are synchronized with macrophage development in rodents, possibly explaining why it is difficult to ontogenically segregate microglia and other macrophage in the CNS.

The first wave begins on day 7.0 of embryo development (E7.0) at the YS blood island (posterior plate mesoderm) and produces primitive progenitor cells around E7.5. Then, they skip the stage of monocytes when differentiating into nucleated erythrocytes and YS macrophages (Ginhoux et al., 2016; Perdiguero et al., 2016). These YS progenitor cells are essentially primary EMPs, and their offspring are YS macrophages. After colonizing throughout the entire embryo, they generate all types of tissue macrophages (Hoeffel et al., 2015b; Ginhoux et al., 2016). EMPs express the colony stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) for survival and differentiation. They are independent of the transcriptional activation gene Myb (Ginhoux et al., 2016; Hoeffel et al., 2015b).

At E8.25, a second hematopoietic wave begins in the YS, generating “late stage” or secondary EMPs (Dick et al., 2022). Secondary EMPs express MYB but not CSF1R (Hoeffel et al., 2015b), suggesting that they have different molecular characteristics and differentiation potentials compared to primary EMPs. A number of macrophages that never leave the YS are derived from secondary EMPs. After colonizing the fetal liver (FL) at E9.5, the secondary EMPs turn into myeloid progenitors, which differentiate into FL monocytes (Hoeffel et al., 2015b; Ginhoux et al., 2016). Then, almost all of the tissues, except the brain, are resided by a large number of FL monocytes. It should be noted that the development of the brain barrier system begins around day 9.5 of the mouse embryo (E9.5), when specialized endothelial cells branch from the vascular plexus of the perineurals to form capillaries that invade the nearby neural tissue (Kadry et al., 2020). Pericytes interact with endothelial cells when neovascularization occurs at E9.5; they begin to form the BBB at around E13.5, preventing FL-monocytes from entering brain tissue (Hoeffel et al., 2015b). When they develop into tissue macrophages, FL-monocytes dilute the original YS-derived macrophages pool and are un distinguishable from each other in adulthood.

Overlapping with the second wave of hematopoiesis, a third wave of “final” hematopoiesis begins in the embryo with the generation of immature hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from the hemogenic endothelium at E8.5 or the aorta-gonads-mesonephros regions at E10.5. Embryonic HSCs seed the FL and give rise to secondary EMPs that generate FL-monocytes (Hoeffel et al., 2015b; Ginhoux et al., 2016). By differentiating into FL-monocytes, HSCs can also contribute to macrophages in tissues except for the brain (Figure 2; Sheng et al., 2015; Ginhoux et al., 2016). Therefore, microglia are primarily derived from primary EMPs, while macrophages from other tissues are contributed by primary EMPs, secondary EMP-derived FL monocytes and HSC-derived FL monocytes. Current studies have largely confirmed that microglia are exclusively seeded from EMPs, and the precursors that infiltrate the prenatal CNS are YS macrophages derived from these EMPs (Figure 2).

sec.p: Once expressing the signal molecular of PU.1 and CSF1R, the EMPs are destined for microglia. These EMPs give rise to YS macrophages before migrating to the parenchyma of the brain. They first become KITLowCX3CR1– intermediate precursors and then develop into more mature KIT–CX3CR1+ macrophages (Kierdorf et al., 2015). However, it is not known exactly how these precursors spread through the embryo and become residents in the parenchyma of the brain during the perinatal period. Two pieces of evidence indirectly supported that blood circulation was responsible for the long-distance transmission to the brain. By utilizing CX3CR1GFP mice, microglia precursors first appear in the interstitial brain at E9.0 and then penetrate the neuroepithelium since E9.5 (Ginhoux et al., 2010). Once in the brain parenchyma, microglia precursors receive guidance signals from the local niche of residence that restrict their differentiation. By P14, the fully mature microglia are capable of expressing marker genes (Butovsky et al., 2014; Bennett et al., 2016). An in vivo single-cell imaging study indicated that microglia have a long lifespan in the mouse neocortex with an average longevity of over 15 months (Füger et al., 2017).

Recruited macrophages are continually replenished by monocytes, while meningeal and perivascular macrophages are derived primarily from embryonic hematopoietic progenitor cells and maintained by self-renewal (Goldmann et al., 2016; Dick et al., 2022). In contrast, macrophages that exist in the choroid plexus have a dual origin, embryonic myeloid precursors and adult HSCs. Most BAM are derived from primitive EMPs throughout adulthood, except for those from secondary EMPs, which migrate from the YS to peripheral tissue through the FL monophyletic cell-derived tissue (Figure 2). Peripheral tissue macrophages express the markers CD64 and Mertk, as opposed to monocytes and microglia.

Blood monocytes are initially derived from HSCs in the FL and subsequently fully derived from bone marrow. Ly6Chi monocytes can enter the brain parenchyma and switch to a patrolling monocyte (Ly6Clow) phenotype during disease or injury (Prinz and Priller, 2014). Most CNS-recruited immune cells, including members of the mononuclear phagocyte system, are transiently confined to the CNS interface and contribute to immune surveillance. They prevent the invasion of pathogens into the CNS and the abnormal proliferation of immune cells. Microglia adjacent to cortical regions with dense and rich synapses help shape synaptic recruitment and the developing vasculature during the perinatal period. Additionally, paravascular microglia migrate along vessels before becoming stationary in adulthood (Garcia et al., 2022). During the late postnatal stage, astrocytes wrap their end-feet around blood vessels until most are covered by adulthood. Microglia preferentially contact the vasculature where complete coverage by astrocytic endfeet is lacking, and the expansion of the astrocytic end-feet is orchestrated by the cessation of microglial motility along the blood vessels.

sec.title: Key Signaling Molecules of Brain Barrier System and Brain-Resident and Recruited Macrophage Development
sec.p: The mechanism for the self-renewal of microglia in the parenchyma is not yet fully understood. CX3C chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1) is an important signaling molecule for macrophage precursors to engraft and disperse in the mouse fetal CNS. In mice lacking CX3CR1 expression, more precursor cells tend to be retained within the YS and FL rather than colonizing the brain and other tissues. Notably, this defect is only observed during the embryonic period, suggesting that other factor), besides CX3CR1, may regulate the cells’ migration. Additionally, microglia are highly reliant on the brain barrier system during development, using the vascular system to migrate to and reside within the brain parenchyma via the CX3CR1 signaling pathway (Mondo et al., 2020).

Microglia differentiation begins in YS EMPs (erythromyeloid precursors). Based on our present knowledge, primary EMPs arise from the mesoderm in the YS independently of a emergence of secondary EMPs in the endothelial hematopoietic region (Perdiguero et al., 2016). Runt-associated transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) is required only for endothelial cell conversion to hematopoietic cells during secondary EMP production (Perdiguero et al., 2016; Table 1). Observations show that generation of primary EMPs is RUNX1 independent. Conversely, fate-mapping analysis utilizing Runx1CreER mice around E7.0 showed the strong labeling of microglia but not macrophages in peripheral tissues. This indicates that microglia indeed come from Runx1+ cells (Ginhoux et al., 2010). Thus, the nature of microglial progenitors is still unclear. Whether the RUNX1 in fate determination of microglial progenitors is necessary remains unsettled.

sec.p: CSF1R signaling is essential for the development and maintenance of microglia (Chitu and Stanley, 2017). During embryogenesis, the proliferation, differentiation and survival of YS macrophages depend on signaling with CSF1R (Ginhoux et al., 2010). In Csf1r mutant mice, no YS macrophages or subsequent tissue-resident macrophages were detectable. Consistent with these findings, the application of CSF1R-specific blocking antibodies was effective for microglia ablation (Hoeffel et al., 2015b). The CSF1R signal may induce a skewed differentiation into myeloid cells by activating PU.1., PU.1 is a myeloid-determining transcription factor that is ubiquitously expressed by hematopoietic cells. Neither resident nor recruited macrophages can be observed in the CNS or other tissues in PU.1 deficient mice (Goldmann et al., 2016). Interestingly, the expression of CSF1R, CSF2R, and CSF3R was downregulated in PU.1–/– mice, and therefore failed to respond to the corresponding cytokines. These results hint at a positive feedback loop between CSF1R and PU.1. In addition, the maintenance of microglial populations in the adult CNS requires a constant CSF1R signal (Buttgereit et al., 2016). Once PU.1 and CSF1R induce myeloid-lineage commitment, microglial progenitors began to differentiate into YS macrophages (Kierdorf et al., 2015; Table 1).

Another transcription factor that is critical for the maturation of resident macrophages is interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8). Knockout of IRF8 results in significant microglial apoptosis in both embryonic and adult mice (Kierdorf et al., 2015). Meanwhile, few meningeal macrophages were observed in Irf8–/– mice, highlighting the essential role of IRF8 in the survival of BAMs (Goldmann et al., 2016).

The erythro-myeloid progenitors in YS generate “premacrophage,” which simultaneously colonize the whole embryo and rapidly diversify in a tissue-specific and chemokine-receptor-dependent manner (Mass et al., 2016). Notably, since E10.25 macrophages initially express microglia-specific genes, such as Sal-like protein (sall) 1 and 3, reminiscent of rapid, environmentally induced lineage commitment (Mass et al., 2016). A transcriptomic study divided microglia development into discrete steps with three important time points (E10.5, E14, and P14) (Bennett et al., 2016). Further investigation should focus on the molecular mechanisms that mediate these shifts.

Transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) is considered a key signaling molecule in microglial development (Butovsky et al., 2014). A mild yet notable elevation in microglial marker gene expression was discerned in primary cultures when comparing microglia cultured with and without TGFβ (Butovsky et al., 2014). In addition, the transcription of some microglia-specific genes could be mimicked even in peritoneal macrophages cultured with TGFβ. Accordingly, studies have shown that TGFβ, cholesterol, and CSF1 secreted by astrocytes coherently support microglial growth in vitro (Butovsky et al., 2014; Bohlen et al., 2017). In line with these studies, Tgfb1 null mice have normal YS macrophages, but are deficient in microglia (Butovsky et al., 2014). Interestingly, TGFβ does not have the capacity to fully recapitulate the brain microenvironment, which is necessary for inducing the microglial differentiation (Bohlen et al., 2017; Gosselin et al., 2017). Thus, TGFβ signals that support microglial survival and differentiation may be necessary but not sufficient (Table 1).

SALL1 is a transcription factor that is specifically expressed in microglia and can be used to identify quiescent microglia (Buttgereit et al., 2016). Sall1 deficiency could result in a remarkable loss of microglial marker genes (e.g., Tmem119, P2ry12) with concomitant upregulation of perivascular macrophage marker genes (Cd163, Lyve1, Cd206, and Cd74) (Buttgereit et al., 2016; Drieu et al., 2022; Table 1). In addition, lipopolysaccharide treatment downregulated Sall1 expression, suggesting that Sall1 may be a key modulator in preserving microglial identity in the context of immune stimulation (Table 1).

Tmem119 is usually regarded as a specific marker in microglia. As a transmembrane protein with uncertain functions, TMEM119 is highly expressed in mice and humans, mainly located on the surface of the cell membrane (Bennett et al., 2016). Due to the fact that BAMs and recruited macrophages do not express this protein, Tmem119 can be considered a useful marker to collaboratively identify and distinguish microglia from other macrophages under physiological conditions as well as after CNS inflammation or injury, such as sciatic nerve injury-induced microglial activation, lipopolysaccharide-induced systemic inflammation, and optic nerve crush injury (Bennett et al., 2016). Notably, caution may be needed regarding the validity of Tmem119 discrimination under certain conditions (Vankriekelsvenne et al., 2022).

Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are essential for the trafficking of immune cells from the perivascular area into the brain parenchyma. Their gelatinase activity in the early stages of neuroinflammation was initially determined in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) in mice, and was further corroborated by the findings of pronounced expression of MMPs in the early active lesions of multiple sclerosis (MS). Additionally, detected by molecular imaging, gelatinase activity has proven to be an effective early indicator of cell infiltration in MS (Ghafouri-Fard et al., 2021). MMP2 (gelatinase A) and MMP9 (gelatinase B) modulate chemokine activity to establish a chemotactic gradient that draws lymphocytes from the perivascular area to the CNS parenchyma, facilitating leukocyte immigration (Song et al., 2015). EMMPRIN (CD147), known as vital for lactate secretion via controlling the monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT-4), is also an MMP inducer expressed by macrophages, endothelial cells and leukocytes, modulating the expression of MMP. Increased levels of EMMPRIN correlate with heightened severity of EAE, whereas its pharmacological ablation mitigates EAE severity (Kaushik et al., 2019). On the contrary, antagonists of MMPs, such as tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 expressed by astrocytes, significantly reduce leukocyte infiltration in the perivascular space.

Research indicates that multiple chemokine receptors are instrumental in directing immune cells through the endothelium to the perivascular space during neuroinflammation. Among them, CC-chemokine receptor 7 and 8 (CCR7 and CCR8) are notably increased during the early relapse stages of EAE. These receptors are also present on inflammatory cells within the perivascular space, where they perform a similar function (Sokol et al., 2018). Chemokine ligands, particularly CCL2 produced by microglia and astrocytes, serve a crucial function. Studies in EAE mice have shown that CCL2– astrocytes barricade CD4+ T cell migration from the perivascular space into the spinal cord parenchyma. Similarly, CXCL10 deficiency in astrocytes led to decreased CD4+ T cell entry into the perivascular space of the spinal cord. Notably, these deficiencies did not affect macrophage accumulation (Dhaiban et al., 2020).

Furthermore, chemokine receptors and their corresponding ligands are responsible for the infiltration of immune cells. Just as it promotes endothelial cell migration, CCL2 orchestrates the movement of inflammatory cells from the perivascular space into the parenchyma. During EAE, both dendritic cells and T cells cross the glial boundary into the parenchyma via CCL2 (Leuti et al., 2021). In a study using a mouse model of viral neuroinflammation, the removal of CCL2 led to the retention of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the perivascular space, thereby delaying the control of viral neuroinflammation (Dubik et al., 2021). CXCL12 and its receptor CXCR4 are critical in regulating inflammatory cell movement into the CNS parenchyma. Studies in EAE have demonstrated that T cells expressing CXCR4 are confined to perivascular spaces rich in CXCL12. During inflammatory conditions, endothelial cells show increased expression of CXCR7, which captures and breaks down CXCL12. When CXCL12 levels decrease in the perivascular space, this creates conditions favorable for inflammation by enabling T cells to migrate into the CNS parenchyma through chemokinetic mechanisms. This process allows immune cells to respond to various chemokines present in the extravascular regions surrounding blood vessels (Song et al., 2015; Joshi and Morley, 2022; Lin et al., 2023).

Significantly, MMP2 and MMP9 are involved in the inactivation of CXCL12 within the perivascular cuff. This action allows immune cells to react to different chemokines expressed beyond the perivascular area. Additionally, these gelatinases selectively degrade various CCL chemokines, such as CCL2, thereby inhibiting the CCR receptor. Therefore, the activity of MMPs at the border region of the parenchyma is crucial in modulating chemotactic signals that traverse this boundary (Song et al., 2017).

During embryonic development, most CNS resident macrophages originate from the yolk sac and grow in specific niches, maintaining their population into adulthood through self-renewal (Goldmann et al., 2016). Recent reviews have delved into the intricate developmental pathways of BAMs and microglia (Brioschi et al., 2020). These cells are derived from different progenitor lineages in the yolk sac, and both lineages exhibit high levels of the fractalkine receptor (CX3CR1) and prolonged lifespan. In contrast to circulating monocytes, BAMs and microglia are generally considered as phagocytes resident within the CNS (Yona et al., 2013; Utz et al., 2020).

BAMs exhibit upregulated genes associated with blood vessel development. BAMs demonstrate distinct characteristics in their lipid and cholesterol metabolism, as well as in their immune response and antigen presentation capabilities compared with microglia (Van Hove et al., 2019). Several genes have been identified as BAM markers, including Apoe, Ms4a7, Ms4a6c, Tgfbi, Mrc1, Dab2, F13a1, Mgl2, and Pf4 (Van Hove et al., 2019; Ochocka et al., 2021; Table 2).

sec.p: BAMs also express conventional macrophage markers such as integrin CD11b, Iba1, Csf1r, and F4/80, at lower levels compared to activated macrophages and circulating monocytes (Korin et al., 2017). Expression of the adhesion molecule CD44 is negligible and can be used to distinguish BAMs from CD44+ blood-borne macrophages within the CNS.

Through a CCL2-dependent manner, monocytes are released from both the bone marrow and the secondary reservoir, spleen. These cells enter the bloodstream with varying lifespans depending on their subset: approximately 1–2 days in mice and 1–7 days in humans (Yona et al., 2013; Teh et al., 2019). In mice, two primary types of blood monocytes have been identified: the “classical” inflammatory monocytes, characterized by Ly6ChighCCR2+CX3CR1low expression, and the “nonclassical” patrolling monocytes, marked by Ly6ClowCCR2+CX3CR1high expression. The nonclassical monocytes develop from classical monocytes in both lymphoid organs and peripheral tissues (Terry et al., 2014). Although Ly6ChighCCR2+CX3CR1low cells are quickly recruited to inflamed tissues via CCR2-mediated mechanisms, patrolling monocytes primarily contribute to maintaining endothelial homeostasis within the vessel lumen (Teh et al., 2019). Nearly all circulating monocytes exhibit a high expression level of CSF1R and receptors for granulocyte-monocyte colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSFR), along with platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM-1), and the β2 and CD11b integrins (Mitchell et al., 2014).

sec.title: Overview of Transcriptome Data Revealed Brain Barrier System–Associated Expression Signatures in Central Nervous System Resident and Recruited Macrophages
sec.p: Microglia, BAMs and recruited macrophages differ in their developmental origins but are not easily distinguished morphologically or functionally. Microglia generally make contact with cerebral blood vessels that lack astrocytic endfeet coverage. Choroid plexus macrophages, meningeal macrophages and perivascular macrophages are directly close to endothelial cells, whereas recruited macrophages from vessels directly interact with the brain barrier system. Recently, a series of studies attempted to classify these cells using the method of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and obtained reliable markers for classification (Van Hove et al., 2019; Ochocka et al., 2021; De Vlaminck et al., 2022). In 2019, Van Hove et al. combined scRNA-seq with other methods to uncover characteristic maker genes in mouse brain. The unique transcriptional properties of nonparenchymal brain macrophages in different borders of the mouse were revealed.

Six major BAM subsets that are distinct from microglia were identified. The SD-BAM cluster was mainly composed of subdural macrophages. However, it showed two subsets called Dlo BAMs and Dhi BAMs, which were divided from dural macrophages. Some dural macrophages in the Dhi BAM cluster were in the same subpopulation as subdural macrophages. CP macrophages were aggregated separately from meningeal macrophages, with the majority clustered in the CPlo BAM and CPhi BAM. It was also noteworthy that a small fraction of CP macrophages (CPepi-BAM) aggregated separately from other BAM or microglia. The expression of microglia marker genes was lower in CPepi-BAMs compared to microglia. This shows that although these CP macrophages were distinct from microglia, they shared a common ontogeny or phenotype. Furthermore, prevalent BAM marker genes included Apoe, Ms4a7, Ms4a6c, Lyz2, and Tgfbi. Similar to microglia, CPepi-BAMs also expressed little or low levels of most of these genes. BAMs also showed tissue-specific features, with marker genes for meninges MHCIIlo BAMs (e.g., Clec4n, Clec10a, and Folr2) or characteristic genes enriched for SD BAMs (e.g., Lyve1, P2rx7, and Egfl7), individual dural BAM subgroups (e.g. Pla2g2d and Cc18) or CP BAMs (e.g., Lilra5 and Ttr). CPepi-BAMs also exhibited a unique transcriptional profile (e.g., Cst7, Gm1673, and Clec7a) (Van Hove et al., 2019). Furthermore, BAMs showed mixed ontogeny, and the subpopulations showed varying capabilities of self-renew after depletion.

Ochocka et al. (2021) demonstrated characteristic molecule of myeloid cells using naive brains. ScRNA-seq of CD11b+ myeloid cells revealed different characteristics in resident and recruited macrophages from naive mice. Through CD11b+ cells, nine clusters were collected from naive female mice, and eight from male mice. The major cluster MG1 (microglia cluster 1) showed distinctive genes expressing highly related to microglia specifically. The genes included Crybb1, Cst3, P2ry12, and Pros1. MG1 was a stable microglia subset (Dubbelaar et al., 2018). Cluster MG2 showed a high expression level of transcription factors including Fos, Egr1, Klf6, Jun, Junb, Jund, and Aft3. Cluster MG3 was characterized by Bhle41, Notch2, and Ncoa3 (Rollins et al., 2015). In addition, three clusters of microglia were acquired from female mice, in which MG5 displayed high expression level of genes related to the process of myelin. The genes included Plp1, Pltp, and Mbp, reminiscent of increased myelin uptake (Theriault et al., 2016). In cluster MG6, the high expression level genes showed Cd63 and Cd9, which are regarded as being highly expressed in extracellular vesicles (Turola et al., 2012). In the pre-microglia cluster, some specific genes of microglia showed a high expression level, including Tmem119, P2ry12, and Crybb1 (Table 2).

Tmem119, Gpr34, P2ry12, Sparc, Selplg, and Cx3cr1 were then applied to identify microglia, while Ly6i and Ly6c2 to macrophages (Bennett et al., 2016), and Ifitm3, Ifitm2, S100a6, and S100a11 to Mo/MΦ (Venteicher et al., 2017). A series of genes (Crip1, Isg15, Ms4a4c, and Lgals3) were highly expressed in all three types. Apoe, Ms4a7, and Mrc1 were expressed in BAMs (Van Hove et al., 2019). Furthermore, F13a1, Dab2, and Pf4 were found to be highly specifically expressed by BAMs. Only in microglia were genes (Tmem119, Gpr34, Olfml3, Sparc Cx3cr1, and P2ry12) highly expressed (Ochocka et al., 2021). In 2022, De Vlaminck et al. revealed the accumulation of microglia in the periventricular region and the response of recruited macrophages. They studied the process of Trypanosoma brucei invading the brain through the border region.

It was first shown that T. brucei invades the brain by progressively penetrating the brain boundary region, disrupting the brain barrier and attracting myeloid cells. Meanwhile, microglia (CD11b+CX3CR1hiCD45lo) and BAMs (CD11b+CX3CR1hiCD45int) are replaced by blood-recruited myeloid cells (CD11b+CD45hi) (Van Hove et al., 2019). Bone marrow-derived cells gradually accumulate in the whole brain. Recruited macrophages progressively lose Ly6B expression and differentiate into CD11bhiLy6Blo macrophages, which accumulate as the disease progresses. It is evident that most CD11b+CD45hi cells accumulate when infected, according to fate mapping performed on Cx3cr1CreER:R26-YFP mice (Goldmann et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013). This implies that, although microglia and BAMs also increase CD45 expression upon infection, they are responsible for a small proportion of CD11b+CD45hi cells.

Further studies have showen that recruited macrophages have a markedly different state compared to the activated microglia. The scRNA-seq was utilized to examine alterations in transcription of microglia while suffering from infection and compared the marker genes with those from recruited macrophages. These cells were selected from naive and infected mice. There was a large alteration in the transcription status of microglia between naive and infected brains, which was confirmed as Sall1+Sparc+C1qb+ clusters. When microglia from infected (Inf Mg) and naive (naive Mg) mice were compared, downregulation of homeostasis genes (Fcrls, Sparc, and P2ry12) (Gautier et al., 2012; Hickman et al., 2013; Butovsky et al., 2014) and upregulation of inflammation-related genes in Inf Mg was observed. Researchers found that the microglia of infected mice and naive mice had expression levels of differential homeostasis genes (P2ry12, Fcrls, and Sparc) and inflammation-related genes (Gautier et al., 2012; Hickman et al., 2013; Butovsky et al., 2014). The infection induced the expression of MHCII transcripts (H2-Aa and Cd74), two specific-expression genes in microglia. Then microglia were re-clustered into eight clusters to further explore their heterogeneity. The fifth cluster showed some disease associated microglia (DAM) related genes (Lilrb4a, Apoe, and Cst7). Cluster six contained some proinflammatory factors, immunosensors and adhesion molecules. Cluster seven contained interferon-induced genes such as Rsad2, Ifit2, and Isg15. Cluster eight represented proliferating microglia consistent with microglial expansion. In addition to microglia, nonclassical monocytes (Ear2+Spn+Ace+), classical monocytes (Ccr2hiChil3hiS100a4hi), and four Sall1-C1qbhi macrophages (MF1–4) were identified. Ly6c2 and Clec12a were highly expressed in the MF1–MF3 clusters, representing recruited macrophages. Microglial genes including Tmem119, Cd9, and Olfml3 were upregulated in MF1. This may indicate brain microenvironment niche imprinting in the recruited macrophages (De Vlaminck et al., 2022). Whereas, low expression of Ly6c2, Clec12a and high expression of Ccl8, Cp, and Vcam1, which are characteristic genes of BAMs were apparent in the MF4 cluster (Van Hove et al., 2019), indicating that BAMs are the source of MF4. Subsequent studies demonstrated that resident macrophages and recruited macrophages differed in profiles of transcription and identified microglia-like cells at the blood–CSF interface of the choroid plexus. A common finding in pathological microenvironments showed that microglia, BAMs and recruited macrophages did not converge into the inflammatory status within the choroid plexus, reflecting limited macrophage plasticity (Van Hove et al., 2019; Table 2).

Microglia, BAMs and macrophages recruited by blood vessels are a hot topic in current research. At present, research on macrophages recruited by inflammation or tumors is still in its infancy. sec.title: Brain Barrier System–Related Central Nervous System Resident and Recruited Macrophage Behavior in Physiological Condition
sec.p: CNS-resident (microglia and BAMs) and recruited macrophages are directly or indirectly related to the brain barrier system. The function and behavior of microglia have been studied in depth. Parenchyma of the brain is scrutinized by microglia every several hours. Through their elaborate processes, such as synaptic gaps, microglia get in touch with most components in the CNS (Fujita and Yamashita, 2021). Although the function of the interaction between microglia and synapses is still being explored, several physiological behaviors have been confirmed to be regulated by the interaction. Recent studies show that microglia contribute to synaptic remodeling and maturation (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Borst et al., 2021; Guedes et al., 2022; Rasia-Filho et al., 2023). Cx3cr1 mutant animals transiently increased the quantity of dendritic spines in certain type of neurons at approximately P15. This phenotype is coincident with a temporary decrease in the number of microglia and an accumulation of immature synapses, resulting in diminished functional connectivity between brain regions and autism-like behavior (Hoshiko et al., 2012). In addition, the microglial signaling of P2RY12 is essential for synaptic plasticity during the critical period of visual acuity, spanning from P21 to P35 in mice. The decline in neuronal plasticity observed in P2ry1-deficient mice aligns with the reduced interactions between microglia and synaptic elements, as well as their morphological reactions to monocular deprivation (Zhang et al., 2023b). Microglia are integral to the processes of complement activation and synaptic pruning, expressing various pivotal complement components such as C1q, C3, and C5 (Stephan et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2021b).

Regarding intercellular relationships, microglia engage with nearly every cell type within the brain, facilitating developmental processes, modulating pain responses, preserving barrier integrity and homeostasis, combating infections, and playing a role in the progression of neuropathological conditions (Frost and Schafer, 2016; Cserép et al., 2020).

Microglia have been confirmed to promote sleep via the activation of inhibitory G protein (Gi protein) signaling lately, which is also associated with a reduction in extracellular norepinephrine (NE) concentration during sleep (Ma et al., 2024). Microglia can regulate sleep/wake state transitions by modulating TRN neuronal activity through ceramide signaling (Liu et al., 2021). Sleep triggers a microglia-mediated enhancement of GABAAR at the synaptic level, a process reliant on microglial TNFα and P2RX7. The selective depletion of TNFα in microglia influences the characteristics of slow waves during NREM sleep and affects the consolidation of procedural memory in tasks that rely on sleep for learning. Consequently, microglia play a pivotal role in orchestrating the intrinsic sleep-related plasticity of synaptic GABAAR, molding the patterns of sleep slow waves, and facilitating the process of memory consolidation (Pinto et al., 2024). Additionally, microglia can regulate the neural network activity of the brain in a region-specific manner instead of the canonical way. Under anesthesia, microglia activate in response to neuronal excitation. This may depend on their unique P2RY12 and downstream intracellular calcium levels to regulate the anesthesia awakening process, rather than relying on C1q-mediated synaptic phagocytosis. Therefore, microglia may be an important participant in the anesthesia process, and their homeostasis is necessary to maintain the anesthetic state (Cao et al., 2023; He et al., 2023; Haruwaka et al., 2024). Microglia can prevent neuronal hyperexcitability and maintain normal sympathetic nerve tension and blood pressure through the interaction mode of the microglial ligand (platelet-derived growth factor) with neuronal receptor (platelet-derived growth factor receptor) (Bi et al., 2022). They can also promote pain by mediating the degradation of the neuronal surrounding network (Tansley et al., 2022). Stress-induced temperature increases can promote abnormal phagocytosis of neural stem cells by microglia, causing neurogenesis disorders (Hoshi et al., 2021).

In the context of phagocytosis and neurogenesis, microglia are capable of engulfing not only dead and dying cells but also, on occasion, healthy living cells within the developing and mature brain. Specifically, during the developmental phase of the cerebellum, microglia actively facilitate phagocytosis-induced death of Purkinje neurons by generating reactive oxygen species (Marin-Teva et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2022). A similar process takes place within the hippocampus, with the generation of reactive oxygen species in microglia being influenced by CD11b and the activation of DNAX-activation protein 12 (DAP12; also known as TYROBP) in microglia (Frost and Schafer, 2016; Lopez-Ortiz et al., 2023). Within the maturing chick retina, microglia produce nerve growth factor (NGF), which interacts with neuronal NGF receptors (referred to as TNFRSF16 and p75NTR), triggering the demise of retinal ganglion cells (Frade and Barde, 1998; Zhang et al., 2024). In the postnatal mouse brain, microglia release insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) to ensure the survival of developing layer 5 neurons as they extend towards their distal CNS destinations (Ueno et al., 2013). The involvement of microglial proliferation and activation in neuropathic pain has been noted (Karavis et al., 2023; Tsuda et al., 2023). Cytokines from dying neurons can stimulate an increase in purinergic receptors (including P2X purinergic receptor 4, P2RX4, P2RX7, or P2RY12) within microglia, leading to enhanced sensitivity to extracellular nucleotides (Tsuda et al., 2017). Cytokine CSF1, released by damaged sensory neurons, seems to stimulate microglia through the CSF1R-DAP12 pathway (Guan et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2021). Once activated, the microglial brain-derived neurotrophic factor binds to its neuronal receptors, causing changes in the neuronal negative ion gradient and resulting in the hyperexcitability of neurons associated with pain (Coull et al., 2005). Concurrently, the microglial enzyme cathepsin S degrades the neuronal surface molecule CX3CL1, which then interacts with microglial CX3CR1 to sustain pain signaling (Chen et al., 2023).

Microglia engage with astrocytes, especially in the context of brain trauma and inflammation. The release of ATP associated with injury creates an ATP gradient emanating from astrocytes, which microglia detect via their P2RY12 purinergic receptor. This detection prompts a swift clustering of microglial processes and triggers cellular migration (Haynes et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2022).

Furthermore, microglia are intimately linked with myelination throughout development, playing a role in regulating axonal bundling within the dorsal corpus callosum (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014). Evidence from pharmacological and genetic ablation studies indicates that microglia in the early postnatal stage are essential for the maturation of oligodendrocyte precursors and the subsequent onset of myelination (Hagemeyer et al., 2017). Under stable physiological conditions, microglia persist in preserving the pool of oligodendrocyte precursors throughout the subsequent life cycle (Hagemeyer et al., 2017). When injury is induced by lysophospholipids, microglia facilitate the process of remyelination through the enhancement of oligodendrocyte differentiation (Miron et al., 2013; Hughes and Stockton, 2021). It is believed that this influence involves microglia expressing MSX3, which releases activin A and engages with activin-A receptors on oligodendrocyte precursors during remyelination (Yu et al., 2015). In addition, microglia engulf myelin, leading to the formation of insoluble aggregates within their lysosomes, which can compromise their functionality throughout the subsequent lifecycle (Kent and Miron, 2024).

Finally, microglia interact with endothelial cells, thereby enhancing the intricacy of the vascular network through the fusion of these endothelial cells (Figure 3). Microglia mediate tip cell fusion following the sprouting of these cells, which is driven by vascular endothelial growth factor signaling (Fantin et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2023). The absence of PU.1 in microglia or in mice with a Csf1 mutation results in a diminished complexity of the cerebral vascular network during early development (Fantin et al., 2017). In zebrafish, microglia are capable of mending laser-induced breaches in brain vessels by physically attaching and applying mechanical force (Liu et al., 2016). Similarly, microglia can seal the ruptured glial boundary or BBB during compression and capillary injury (Roth et al., 2014). During chronic injury, the retraction of microglial processes driven by ATP is facilitated through the downregulation of P2RY12 and the simultaneous upregulation of the GS-coupled adenosine receptor A2A (Orr et al., 2009).

In addition, microglia perform several physiological chores such as synapse monitoring, complement pruning, neurogenesis and neuronal connectivity, surveillance in parenchyma. sec.p: Microglia are crucial in the regulation of the brain’s vascular network, but the extent to which their functions are specific to perivascular associate microglia is not well-defined. For instance, during embryonic development, microglia are typically found at vascular junctions. The elimination of all microglial cells has been observed to lead to a decrease in the complexity of the vascular structure. (Fantin et al., 2010). Additionally, as previously mentioned, the microglia-astrocyte interaction modulates microglial migration. Before the endfeet of astrocytes enwrap the vasculature, microglia migrate towards the blood vessels to precisely modulate the reorganization of the entire brain vascular network, aiding in preserving the integrity of the BBB (Mondo et al., 2020).

BAMs are involved in the surveillance and purification of CSF. Additionally, they contribute to the removal of metabolites originating from the CNS, as well as antigens and infiltrating microorganisms (Gerganova et al., 2022). A previous study indicates that BAMs can swiftly absorb various substances (including dextran, ovalbumin, ferritin, and horseradish peroxidase) delivered either into the brain or throughout the body, thereby underpinning their function in filtering CSF (Santisteban et al., 2020). Bulk RNA sequencing of brain macrophages revealed heightened expression of genes associated with lipid metabolism and cholesterol storage in perivascular macrophages compared to microglia (Van Hove et al., 2019). Under homeostatic conditions, only a restricted number of bone marrow-derived macrophages (recruited macrophages) are present at the host interfaces in the CNS.

sec.title: Central Nervous System Resident and Recruited Macrophage Behavior in Pathological Conditions
sec.p: The versatility between recruited and resident macrophages has been observed in several diseases (Yamasaki et al., 2014; Prinz et al., 2019; Table 3). Specifically, microglia are closely associated with the brain barrier system in stroke, glioma, demyelination, and degenerative diseases (Stankovic et al., 2016; Hattori, 2023). Studying the ontogeny and functional status with the underlying mechanisms at different stages and diseases is crucial for understanding the heterogeneity of these macrophages.

sec.title: Inflammatory demyelination
sec.p: Macrophages are the dominant cell type within the damaged areas of the CNS in MS patients, regardless of clinical progression or lesion subtype. Therefore, MS disease-modifying therapies significantly impact the functions of macrophages, which are a crucial component of their therapeutic effect (Fischer et al., 2019; Ivan et al., 2021; Spiteri et al., 2022).

Now it is believed that microglia perform diverse, but mainly detrimental roles in MS. Microglial activation is a common pathogenesis of MS (Block et al., 2007). Mounting evidence indicates that microglial activation in MS patients precedes BBB disruption. Compromised BBB integrity, an initial characteristic of multiple sclerosis (MS), exacerbates MS progression (Sweeney et al., 2018). In fact, research has revealed that depleting microglia significantly ameliorates BBB impairment in models of EAE (Yu et al., 2022). Specifically, in both acute and chronic plaques of MS autopsy specimens, the number of dysfunctional microglia (miR-126a-5p–) is positively correlated with impairment of BBB integrity. Indeed, the loss of miR-126a-5p in microglia exacerbates BBB leakage and enhances the severity of EAE (Yu et al., 2022). Whereas, Auranofin, by targeting the microglia miR-126a-5p/MMP9 axis, preserves BBB integrity and ameliorate MS severity (Yu et al., 2022). Intriguing, a former study also reported that microglia play a bidirectional role in BBB integrity during peripheral inflammatory responses. Initially, it maintains the BBB during the compensated stage, whereas, microglial activation aggravates BBB disruption during the uncompensated periods of inflammatory demyelination (Haruwaka et al., 2019). In the presence of persistent inflammation, microglia engage in the phagocytosis of astrocyte endfeet, contributing to blood–brain barrier breakdown (Stankovic et al., 2016). Additionally, microglia also affect the brain barrier system through interactions with the adaptive immune system. Microglia-derived CCL2/CCL8 chemokines mediate the infiltration of CD8+ T cells and tissue damage in RIBI mice by binding to CCR2+/CCR5+ on CD8+T cells (Shi et al., 2023).

The involvement of BAMs in MS has not been extensively acknowledged. However, several studies have shown that BAMs play roles at each stage of MS and contribute to determining the types of lesions in the CNS (Derk et al., 2021; Merlini et al., 2022; Ostkamp et al., 2022). By comparison, recruited macrophages play a detrimental role in the pathology of the disease. Accordingly, strategies to limit this infiltrating behavior can alleviate MS symptoms in animal models (Mishra et al., 2016). Studies using scanning electron microscopy have demonstrated that recruited macrophages, which cluster around the nodes of Ranvier initiate demyelination. Conversely, microglia facilitate tissue repair by clearing away myelin debris (Yamasaki et al., 2014; Yong et al., 2022).

sec.title: Vascular diseases
sec.p: Cytokines released by microglia, such as IL-6 and TNF-α, fuel the pathogenesis of dementia (Block et al., 2007). Research indicates that patients with vascular dementia have higher serum IL-6 levels (Dukic et al., 2016), reflecting inflammatory factors in the process of VCI (vascular cognitive impairment). Astrocytic endfeet were disrupted following microglial activation and proinflammatory cytokine release, causing alteration of vascular permeability in cerebral amyloid angiopathy and hyperhomocysteinemia models of VCI (Sudduth et al., 2017). Perivascular BAMs, as resident immune cells distinct from microglia, similarly release reactive oxygen species, leading to vascular-related and cognitive dysfunction (Uekawa et al., 2023). In cerebral ischemia models, a specific BAM subpopulation was found to express elevated levels of MHCII-associated antigen presentation molecules, including H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, and Cd74, indicating that BAMs regulate adaptive immune responses after ischemic stroke (Blank-Stein and Mass, 2023). BAMs also regulate the CSF flow rate, thereby participating in the clearance of extracellular matrix proteins. Through MRI and light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, it was observed in vivo that the CSF flow rate decreased after BAM depletion (Drieu et al., 2022).

sec.title: Alzheimer’s disease
sec.p: Microglial activation is a prominent characteristic of neuroinflammation in neurodegenerative disorders (Ueno et al., 2013). While the roles of other macrophage populations in both mouse models and AD patients are still unclear, research focusing on BAMs has emphasized their importance in amyloid-beta (Aβ) clearance, suggesting their potential as therapeutic targets (Sun et al., 2024; Mary et al., 2024). Disease-associated inflammatory macrophages (DIMs) have been discovered in regions distributed with mature microglia (Silvin et al., 2022). These cells originate from monocytes and are TREM2-independent. DIM cell populations mainly accumulate in the hippocampus, meninges, basolateral amygdala, and cortex of AD model mice, and are located near Aβ aggregates. Their numbers increase significantly with aging and play a unique role in degenerative disease. Another study demonstrated that perivascular BAMs promote microglia phagocytosis via SPP1, resulting in abnormal or irregular ingestion of synapses in the hippocampus of AD mouse models (De Schepper et al., 2023). These findings offer compelling evidence that the interaction between BAMs and microglia causes synapse loss in AD, and highlight macrophage dysfunction as the culprit behind memory loss in AD.

sec.title: Parkinson’s disease
sec.p: In Parkinson’s disease (PD), BAMs are essential for presenting antigens, activating T cells, and facilitating the infiltration of inflammatory cells (Zou et al., 2019; Bogale et al., 2021). In post-mortem PD brain tissue, CD3+ T cells were found near CD68+ BAMs in perivascular spaces (Schonhoff et al., 2023). BAMs, but not microglia, contribute to α-synuclein related neuroinflammation, serving as antigen-presenting cells that trigger a CD4+ T cell response (Schonhoff et al., 2023). While the overall monocyte count remains unchanged in PD patients, these cells exhibit increased proliferation, reduced activation response, and altered phagocytosis (Nissen et al., 2019). Additionally, monocytes from PD patients show elevated expression of the FAS/FAS ligand system, which may enhance both myeloid cell recruitment and cytokine secretion (Gerganova et al., 2022). These patients also demonstrate increased levels of CCL2 in the blood and abnormal responses of CCR2+ monocytes (Ivan et al., 2021).

sec.title: Infection
sec.p: Related studies have shown that monocytes are massively recruited to the brain during parasite infection (Costa et al., 2022; De Vlaminck et al., 2022; Quintana et al., 2022). Through scRNA-seq, researchers discovered that recruited macrophages exhibited unique transcriptional patterns (e.g., immune receptors) apart from resident macrophages, indicating a distinct response of macrophage to ongoing tissue inflammation. Meanwhile, tissue-resident macrophages, which are programmed to maintain tissue homeostasis, appear to have epigenetic constraints that limit their functional flexibility (Lavin et al, 2014).

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This review has some limitations. It mainly focused on CNS resident macrophages, at least partly because of the lack of study on monocyte-derived macrophages (recruited macrophages). Furthermore, due to the lack of effective tools to distinguish BAMs derived from different sources, especially in pathological conditions, certain previous findings regarding the function of BAMs may yield mixed results, requiring careful interpretation and review.

sec.title: Discussion and Prospect
sec.p: (1) In physiological conditions, the types of immune cells change with regional changes. The complexity of immune cells decreases with increasing proximity to the brain parenchyma. Macrophages residing around the boundaries of the CNS exert diverse effects on the brain barrier system.

As the permeability of the brain barrier system changes, so does the abundance and composition of macrophages in the border region. For example, the dura mater can connect directly to the bone marrow of the skull through specific microchannels in the intracranial vasculature (Herisson et al., 2018; Cugurra et al., 2021; Mazzitelli et al., 2022). Similar to the CP, it also contains a number of immune cell subsets including monocytes, lymphocytes, granulocytes, dendritic cells and BAMs (Mundt et al., 2019a; van Hove et al., 2019; Schaflick et al., 2021). Monocytes from the periphery can only enter the dura mater and CP and replenish BAMs in situ while simultaneously elevating MHCII expression (Mrdjen et al., 2018; Mundt et al., 2019b; van Hove et al., 2019). Whereas, the inner meninges and perivascular space are prevented from patrolling by recruited macrophages (Mundt et al., 2019a, b; van Hove et al., 2019). Therefore, the diversity of macrophages declines with increasing spatial proximity to the brain parenchyma.

Furthermore, CNS-recruited macrophages control the CNS boundaries. Almost all of the CNS-recruited macrophages are confined to CNS interfaces. They cross these structures only transiently at homeostasis. In contrast, resident macrophages have long-term effects. Certain subsets of macrophages mediate the neuroinflammatory response by promoting immune cell recruitment and infiltration in PD (Schonhoff et al., 2023), while others maintain barrier integrity and reduce vascular injury by inhibiing matrix metalloproteinases, complements or upregulating PDGF (De Vlaminck et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Weng et al., 2024). Thus, BAMs can be modulated to protect the brain barrier system, thereby protecting the CNS.

(2) The phenotypes of macrophages under certain pathological conditions remain to be clarified. In addition, lack of efficient and specific delivery tools targeting macrophages is another obstacle. Due to the lack of plausible markers, distinguishing microglia from other macrophages in inflammatory as well as neoplastic disorders has not been solved yet. The heterogeneity of macrophage populations in health and disease remains largely elusive (Masuda et al., 2019; Friebel et al., 2020; Klemm et al., 2020; Absinta et al., 2021). Encouragingly, the advances in single-cell sequencing techniques coupled with stem cell-derived organoids contribute to deciphering macrophage heterogeneity and dissect their functions (Dumas et al., 2021).

Inducible genetic tools with increasing specificity and intricacy are needed to distinguish microglia, BAMs and monocytes in preclinical models. Currently, a major technical barricade is the lack of tools to specifically manipulate macrophage subtypes in transgenic animals. Currently, we still lack high-efficiency vectors for microglia transduction in vivo. In 2022, a series of new rAAV vectors with higher efficiency for microglia transduction in vivo and in vitro were developed through directed evolution strategies. Furthermore, scRNA-seq demonstrated that AAV-MG variants mediate specific and efficient transgene delivery with no microglial hyperactivation. New tools to investigate sensors and effectors of microglia will certainly be available based on the AAV variants (Lin et al., 2022). In vivo observation and gene editing of microglia will certainly contribute to an augmentation of feasible tools in research on microglia biology and gene therapy.
(3) More appropriate models and systems are needed to dissect functions of macrophages.

Due to the sensitivity of macrophages, especially microglia, to external stimulus and the sophisticate architecture of the brain barrier system, it is necessary to combine whole animal models with in vitro culture systems to investigate the cells’ role in the brain barrier system. Transcriptomic analysis of human and mouse macrophages has revealed the differential expression profiles of species, which include genes responsible for phagocytosis and immune function. A plausible strategy is to utilize appropriate human-based models and humanized cells to overcome some of the limitations of animal models (Brownjohn et al., 2018; McQuade et al., 2018; Warden et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a), and to capture the physiological and genetic functions of macrophage (Galatro et al., 2017; Gosselin et al., 2017; Madore et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Paolicelli et al., 2022). We advocate for the use of human sources of biological material in basic research, which may aid in developing innovative therapeutics that can be more easily translated to clinical applications (Smith and Dragunow 2014; Bjornson-Hooperv et al., 2022; De Vlaminck et al., 2022; Rebejac et al., 2022; Schonhoff et al., 2023).

Meanwhile, it is noteworthy that despite the variations in macrophage characteristics between humans and model organisms (Van Hove et al., 2019; Mass, 2023; Bao et al., 2024), the infiltration of monocytes into the CNS occur similarly in both humans and model animals under pathological conditions (Pombo Antunes et al., 2021; Schonhoff et al., 2023). The characteristics of disease-associated macrophages, encompassing those derived from microglia and monocytes, remain conserved across species in the aging brain (Silvin et al., 2022). Thus, a more cautious interpretation of these results from humans and model animals is required. It is therefore recommended that further studies utilizing rodent models in conjunction with, where feasible, human specimens or neuropathological analysis of cadaveric material (Guttikonda et al., 2021; Popova, et al., 2021; Tewari et al., 2021).
(4) High spatial-temporal resolution, highly sensitive and low-risk approaches contribute to clarifying the different characters of CNS macrophages.

Neuroimaging has evolved from invasive recordings to non-invasive approaches (Absinta et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021a; Yen et al., 2023), which reduces potential risks and can be intuitively detected with both temporal and spatial resolution (Loosen et al., 2024). We can acquire detailed brain imaging of awake, functioning humans by employing magnetic fields and radio waves, detecting the emitted positrons or monitoring the electrical and magnetic activity evoked by neural activity (Finn et al., 2023). An in-depth examination of disease progression and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) insights obtained from scans can aid in delineating the correlation between clinical symptoms and neural activity in individuals with psychiatric and neurological illnesses (Yin et al., 2022; Finn et al., 2023; Kotoula et al., 2023). In some cases, specific tissue components can be imaged using detectable biomarkers; however, the restricted penetration of the BBB limits the labeling of macrophages within the CNS (Kim et al., 2021a). Nevertheless, MRI detection has been successfully applied to detect macrophages, that cross the blood–CSF barrier, in the choroid plexus (Wang et al, 2024). Imaging technology with higher tissue accessibility and resolution coupled with more sensitive and highly specific probes, is thus needed.

Notably, utilizing time-of-flight mass cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, single-nuclei RNA sequencing and comprehensive analytical approaches, investigators have delineated the transcriptional landscapes of macrophages in the CNS and identified differential gene expressions among them (Sankowski et al., 2019; Lopes et al., 2022; Kearns et al., 2023; Tuddenham et al., 2024). Integrating multi-omics technologies to fine-tune the expression and regulation of CNS macrophages is expected to provide a comprehensive and in-depth functional panorama.
(5) The understanding of different types and lineages of macrophages in (patho) physiological conditions is still limited. Identification of novel minor subsets of macrophages is ongoing.

Beyond their essential functions in embryogenesis and homeostasis maintenance, both resident and newly recruited macrophages are increasingly recognized as key modulators in CNS disorders (Thion et al., 2018; Van Hove et al., 2019; Ivan et al., 2021). Microglia, BAMs, and recruited macrophages perform differently under the same conditions in CNS disorders (De Vlaminck et al. 2022; Rebejac et al., 2022; Schonhoff et al., 2023). Owing to their high heterogeneity, macrophages are capable of adopting various phenotypes and exhibit a complex array of both shared and distinct markers under pathological conditions (Gordon and Taylor, 2005; Li and Barres, 2018). For instance, in the brains of mouse AD models, the disease-associated microglia can be further subdivided into two distinct subsets: a neuroprotective subset marked by embryonically originated TREM2-dependent disease associated microglia, and an inflammatory subset identified by TREM2-expressing macrophages derived from monocytes (Silvin et al., 2022). These studies broaden our perspective from disease-associated microglia to disease-associated macrophages, further explaining the heterogeneity and functional diversity of macrophages in the CNS. In addition, macrophages may interact with one another. In a study of PD, the depletion of BAMs resulted in reduced activation of microglia along with a decreased number of infiltrating monocytes capable of differentiating into macrophage, reminiscent of BAMs in cell recruitment (Schonhoff et al., 2023).
